topicName: OWASP Top 10 in Rails (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, Mass Assignment)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Securing Ruby on Rails Applications Against the OWASP Top 10"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ruby on Rails provides a secure foundation out of the box, often following the principle of secure by default. However, understanding common vulnerabilities like SQL Injection (SQLi), Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), and Mass Assignment is critical for every Rails developer to build truly robust applications."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. SQL Injection (SQLi)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"SQL Injection occurs when user input is directly concatenated into database queries, allowing attackers to manipulate the SQL statement. While Rails' ActiveRecord protects against SQLi in most finder methods, raw SQL fragments or dynamic column names can introduce vulnerabilities."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"# VULNERABLE: String interpolation allows SQL injection
User.where("name = '#{params[:name]}'")

# SECURE: Using parameterized queries
User.where("name = ?", params[:name])

# SECURE: Using hash conditions
User.where(name: params[:name])"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"XSS happens when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper validation or escaping, allowing malicious scripts to execute in the victim's browser. Modern Rails views (ERB) escape all output by default."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"# SECURE: ERB automatically escapes HTML
<%= @user.biography %>

# VULNERABLE: Using raw or html_safe bypasses protection
<%= raw @user.biography %>
<%= @user.biography.html_safe %>"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"CSRF forces an authenticated user to execute unwanted actions on a web application in which they are currently authenticated. Rails prevents this using Synchronizer Token Patterns built directly into controllers."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"# Ensure your ApplicationController includes protect_from_forgery
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  protect_from_forgery with: :exception
end

# Rails forms automatically include the CSRF meta tags and token
# <%= csrf_meta_tags %>"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Mass Assignment"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mass assignment vulnerabilities occur when an application passes a hash of parameters directly to an ActiveRecord model to initialize or update attributes, potentially allowing users to modify sensitive fields like admin status."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"# VULNERABLE: Passing params directly allows updating any attribute
user = User.new(params[:user])

# SECURE: Using Strong Parameters to whitelist attributes
private

def user_params
  params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :password)
end"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always use parameterized queries or hash conditions in ActiveRecord."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid using html_safe or raw helpers on user-supplied content."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep protect_from_forgery enabled in your application controller."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Enforce strong parameters strictly for all incoming model attributes."}]
